messages.subject: 2017 2-week summer workshop - Analyzing High Throughput Sequencing Data
messages.subject_clean: 2017 2-week summer workshop - Analyzing High Throughput Sequencing Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am pleased to announce that we will be running a two-week summer workshop on analyzing high-throughput sequencing data! This workshop will run from June 26-July 8th, 2017, and it is an continuation of the two-week NGS workshop run at Michigan State University since 2010. (You can read about the 2015 workshop here: http://ivory.idyll.org/blog/2015-small-batch.html.)

With our move to UC Davis, this year we will be able to take 3-4x as many applicants as in previous years!

ANGUS: Analyzing High Throughput Sequencing Data

June 26-July 8, 2017

University of California, Davis

	• Zero-entry - no experience required or expected!
	• Hands-on training in using the UNIX command line to analyze your sequencing data.
	• Friendly, helpful instructors and TAs!
	• Summer sequencing camp - meet and talk science with great people!
	• Now in its eighth year!

The workshop fee will be $500 for the two weeks, and on-campus room and board is available for $500/week. Applications will close March 17th. International and industry applicants are more than welcome!

Please see http://ivory.idyll.org/dibsi/ANGUS.html for more information, and contact dibsi.t...@gmail.com if you have questions or suggestions.

If I'm fitting a set of parameters A and B using ML, where B is subject to constraints, can I estimate the standard error (SE) of A if the ML solution puts B on its constraint (i.e., its variance ends up negative)? I know that in such cases you can compute SE of A, but is there a nuanced interpretation of A's SE in this case?

Many thanks for any insights (or links to particularly accessible resources) you can offer!!

messages.subject: Aggregating daily data
messages.body_plain:
Hello

My input is a wide data.frame giving daily data about a respondent for the entire year (see attachment). The data frame need not have 365 columns because data for some days are missing.

I want to aggregate the daily data to weekly data following the convention for week number summarized here (http://www.epochconverter.com/weeks/2016). Basically, Week-1 is from Jan 4th 2016 to Jan 10th 2016. Week-2 is from Jan 11 to Jan 17th. And so on.

The final data set should have 52 columns where each column gives the simple average for that week.

I can manually aggregate the columns using 52 lines of code (one line per week). But that would be foolish.

Any ideas how to automate the above process?

Thanks so much.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Aggregating daily data
messages.body_plain:
Make your wide data long and it's not so much of an issue really.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

a <- read_csv("~/Downloads/input.csv")

a %>%
gather(Date, Value, -ID) %>%
mutate(Date = mdy(Date),
Week = week(Date),
Value = as.numeric(gsub("%", "", Value, fixed = TRUE))/100) %>% # http://stackoverflow.com/questions/29312622/how-to-convert-all-percentage-data-in-r-to-decimal
group_by(ID, Week) %>%
summarize(ValueWeek = mean(Value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
spread(Week, ValueWeek)

If you are missing data for an entire week, you might need to do some more work to ensure all 52 columns are made. Also, R isn't too happy with numbered columns so you could change those or just leave it long and do your analysis from there. Why do you want the wide dataframe back? Displaying a table with that much information would be very hard to read.

B

messages.subject: Reworking a glmer.nb model, hoping to double check my solution
messages.subject_clean: Reworking a glmer.nb model, hoping to double check my solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi all-

I've been trying to get a glmer.nb model to converge with various levels of success.  I just succeeded, but at this point, I've done so many strange things to it I'd like to run it past some of you who are more familiar with this kind of model manipulation. Since apparently I've been #blessed for the entirety of my PhData thus far with a non-converging model.

Original model:
PG1<- glmer.nb(grains ~  restored + grazed + bees +logpopsize+ (1|Site) , data=pen)
(where grazed, restored are factors, and grains, bees, and log pop size are all numeric within the range of 1 to about 500)

Warning messages:
1: In checkConv(attr(opt, "derivs"), opt$par, ctrl = control$checkConv,  :
  Model failed to converge with max|grad| = 0.00118593 (tol = 0.001, component 1)
2: In checkConv(attr(opt, "derivs"), opt$par, ctrl = control$checkConv,  :
  Model failed to converge with max|grad| = 0.00131464 (tol = 0.001, component 1)

The googlewebs gave me a few sets of responses, varying from - ignore this warning, to do all of these: rescale/check gradients/reoptimize/check singularity.
So, the gradient comparison looks good ( #[1] 2.697223e-06, where 0.001 is the threshold) singularity looks good (#[1] 0.1183687, so not wicked tiny #e-06) , didn't need to be rescaled. What did work was finding a new starting point.
(here is the link for where I've mostly been pulling testing code from https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/33653_57fc7b8e5d484c909b615d8633c01d51.html)

What I did:
ss <- getME(PG1,c("theta","fixef"))
PG1a <- update(PG1,start=ss,control=glmerControl(optCtrl=list(maxfun=2e4)))

When I run it now, it smiles, gives me answers, and doesn't bleed red all over my screen!

**So here is my question:  Am I correct in following that code to find a new starting point? That it doesn't do anything weird to the actual structure or interpretation of my negative binomial general linear model?  It worries me that the code ignored the negative binomial aspect of the original model in the control=  section.  And final question, once I do that is there a specific way to reveal that I did that in a paper. **

and you know the secondary question... is there a simpler way? I've got 6 more models per treatment *3 plants to futz with and then compare...

Thanks all, I really appreciate everything that DRUG does!
Jenny

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenny,

If I'm understanding this correctly, I think the only thing that's happening is that when you update your model you're telling it to start the fitting process (however glmer.nb does that) in a different, more optimal part of parameter space. So you're still fitting the same model, but you're just doing it a bit more intelligently, so you don't get the error messages. Look at the actual "ss" object and see what starting values are being used for the various parameters. I would imagine you could feed those values to a "start" argument in your original call to glmer.nb. That might save you some steps in your code. That would also verify that you are fitting the same model you thought you were, except you're just starting the fitting process at a different set of values such that you don't get errors.

To me at least, this sort of code optimization wouldn't be something worthy of describing in a paper's methods section. Having these sorts of fitting issues is common depending on how the fitting is actually done, and you often have to fiddle with starting values and such. So, I'd say it would still be accurate and complete to say something to the effect of, "We fit models using the function 'glmer.nb' in R..."

Someone else here correct me if I'm way off base. In addition, Jaime's suggestion to directly inquire on the r mixed models list might give you more peace of mind that you're doing things correctly.

Best,
Evan

messages.subject_clean: Reworking a glmer.nb model, hoping to double check my solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenny,

I would add one word of warning - if the optimization is getting stuck, it could be a sign of some pathology in your model. I would say do not ignore the warnings, but try to figure out what they mean. Your solution is doing two things at once: changing the starting values and changing the max iterations. I would change one at a time to see which is making the difference, because that could indicate better what is going on.

If you are going to play with different starting values, I would say run it with many many (100+) starting values and ensure the model converges to the same-ish place each time. If you use different starting values and get different estimates, you need to pause and figure out what is wrong with your model.

For reporting purposes, make the code and data available with your paper, so people can see exactly what you did. Many reviewers are not going to care, but it is important you have some record of how someone could reproduce your findings.

Matt
